hints: Start by working out which halogen fits the Mr of 137, remember the general mass is 14n + 1 + Ar(X).
Once you find n = 4 and X = bromine, draw out CH3-CHBr-CH2-CH3 and look closely at carbon 2 with its four different groups.
For elimination, think about removing H from C1 versus C3 to make the double bond in different places, then check if one of those alkenes can show E/Z isomerism.
walkthrough:
**Identify the halogen and chain length**

Great start, let us find what Y actually is. Use the Mr equation for $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+1}\text{X}$.

$$M_r = 12n + (2n+1) + A_r(\text{X}) = 14n + 1 + A_r(\text{X}) = 137$$

$$14n + A_r(\text{X}) = 136$$

**Test the halogens**

Try each halogen mass. Only bromine works nicely.

$$\text{If X = Br, } A_r = 80: 14n = 136 - 80 = 56, \text{ so } n = 4$$

This gives a straight chain of 4 carbons with Br on C2: $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, which is 2-bromobutane.

**Check statement 1, chirality**

Look at C2. It is bonded to four different groups: $\text{H}$, $\text{Br}$, $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$.

That makes C2 a chiral centre, so statement 1 is correct.

**Check statement 2, structural isomers from elimination**

Elimination of HBr can remove H from two different neighbouring carbons.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{CH}_3 \rightarrow \text{CH}_2\text{=CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3 \text{ (but-1-ene) or } \text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH}_3 \text{ (but-2-ene)}$$

These have the double bond in different positions, so they are structural isomers. Statement 2 is correct.

**Check statement 3, geometrical isomers**

Now look at but-2-ene, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH}_3$. Each C of the double bond has two different groups ($\text{H}$ and $\text{CH}_3$).

So it can exist as cis (Z) and trans (E) forms. Statement 3 is correct. All three statements are correct.

options.A: Option A states 1, 2 and 3 are all correct. We proved Y is 2-bromobutane, C2 is chiral, elimination gives but-1-ene and but-2-ene as structural isomers, and but-2-ene shows cis-trans isomerism.
options.B: Any option with only 1 and 2 is incomplete. Students choose this if they forget that but-2-ene has two different groups on each alkene carbon and so shows E/Z isomerism.
options.C: Any option omitting 1 is wrong. Students choose this if they miss that C2 in 2-bromobutane has four different substituents and is therefore chiral.
options.D: Any option with only 1 is wrong. This comes from thinking elimination gives only one alkene, forgetting that H can be lost from C1 to give but-1-ene or from C3 to give but-2-ene.
